name: Irimu
other_names: Ilimu | irimu | Chaga irimu | Kamba eimu
origin: Kikuyu, Kenya (kin name among the Chaga, Tanzania)
looks: A huge long-haired man-shaped ogre, sometimes one-footed and walking with a stick, with a body nearly proof against weapons.
behavior: Eats people, luring girls and wives into his house; in tales he is tricked, trapped in a pit, or killed where he is soft under the arm.
license_note: Folk-tale ogre recorded by Routledge (1910) and noted by Werner (1933) as the Chaga irimu; our description is original.
sensitivity_note: Ogre of folk tales, not a sacred being. Owner asked for Kenya. Do not dress a faction as Kikuyu. Routledge's text also shows a benevolent N'jenge kin, so keep the ogre only.
reads_at_16x20: yes: huge shaggy silhouette with a walking stick

name: Mukun'ga M'bura (rainbow water monster)
looks: A water monster that shows itself as a man or a snake, linked in the tales to the rainbow.
behavior: Swallows people, cattle and whole homesteads; a warrior cuts it open and frees all it swallowed.
license_note: Folk tale in Routledge (1910). Spelling of the name is as printed there.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Rainbow lore may touch Kikuyu religion; keep it a generic marsh serpent.
reads_at_16x20: yes: long serpent with a banded back

name: Chemosit
looks: A bogey that is half man, half bird, standing on one leg, with a mouth glowing red like a lamp.
behavior: Sings sweetly at night to lure children away, who are never seen again.
license_note: Folk bogey; some writers merge it with the Nandi bear (kerit). Both pages are Wikipedia, so treat as one source.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source (two Wikipedia pages). The article says adult Kalenjin do not seriously believe in it, but it is a Kalenjin children's bogey; keep it generic.
reads_at_16x20: yes: one-legged bird-man with a glowing mouth

name: Kerit (Nandi bear)
other_names: Nandi bear | Koddoelo | Ngoloko | Duba | Nkampit
looks: A hulking, sloping-backed beast taller than a hyena, with reddish hair and long feet, able to stand on its hind legs.
behavior: Hunts at night and, in the stories, eats only the brains of its victims; likely a mix of real animals and legend.
license_note: Cryptid; written reports date from about 1905-1914. Older local story unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source (two Wikipedia pages). Sightings are often explained as misidentified hyenas.

name: Popobawa
looks: A shapeshifting evil spirit named for the bat-wing shadow it casts, with a sulfur smell sometimes noted.
behavior: Visits households at night and attacks; panics rise and fall with politics and ease with exorcism and charms.
license_note: First reports are from 1965 (Pemba), peak 1995: modern origin, folklore age unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Living belief tied to real fear, assault and politics; the most feared attacks are sexual. Not suited to a game enemy; listed so the owner sees it.
reads_at_16x20: yes: bat-winged shadow, but the story is a poor fit

name: Buda
looks: A person said to turn into a hyena at night, hiding a human identity.
behavior: Said to harm with the evil eye and attack in hyena form; victims use amulets and priests.
license_note: Folk belief; a plain hyena-man could be written from scratch.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. RED: the belief is aimed at real groups (blacksmiths, Beta Israel) and fuels stigma. Never use the name. A generic hyena-man should carry no Ethiopian label.
reads_at_16x20: yes as a generic hyena, no as Buda

name: Zimwi
origin: Bantu peoples of eastern and southern Africa (Zulu, Swahili and kin)
looks: An ogre that is never merely human, often able to take human shape.
behavior: Carries off and swallows children and girls; found in tales almost everywhere.
license_note: Folk-tale ogre class described by Werner (1933).
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Folk-tale ogre; generic name across many languages.
reads_at_16x20: yes: broad ogre silhouette with a sack

name: Ninki Nanka
looks: A big reptile shaped like a crocodile-headed, horse- or donkey-bodied beast, or a giant snake.
behavior: Lives in swamps and rivers; a deadly stare is said to be turned aside with mirrors.
license_note: First documented in a 1906 colonial report, no premodern text: folklore age unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Folk cryptid; widely used in fiction.

name: Adze
looks: A firefly in the wild that becomes human when caught.
behavior: Slips through cracks at night to drink blood and possess people.
license_note: Ewe folk belief; earliest records not shown on the page: unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Living belief; accusations of being an adze fall on women, the elderly and the poor. Use the firefly swarm only; never the possessed human.
reads_at_16x20: yes as a glowing firefly swarm

name: Sasabonsam
looks: A tree-dwelling being with iron teeth, long hair, bloodshot eyes and feet pointing both ways.
behavior: Perches in high boughs, dangles its legs to snare hunters and strikes from above.
license_note: Recorded among enslaved Akan in 1774 (Long); older roots likely.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Akan folk belief with ongoing local currency; keep it a generic forest ambusher.
reads_at_16x20: yes: dangling legs from above, iron fangs

name: Grootslang
origin: Richtersveld and Orange River, South Africa
looks: A giant serpent about 12 to 15 meters long, in some tales with diamonds for eyes.
behavior: Guards a cave of treasure and preys on cattle; one writer argued it grew from python sightings.
license_note: Earliest source on the page: Cornell, 1920. Folklore age unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Cryptid lore, widely used in fiction.
reads_at_16x20: yes: huge snake with gem eyes

name: Impundulu
looks: A person-sized black-and-white bird that calls storms with its wings; sometimes a handsome young man.
behavior: A blood-craving witch's familiar passed down a family line that strikes the witch's enemies.
license_note: Folk belief, long recorded.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Living belief. The page records a 2005 case where a man killed a child he took for an impundulu. Use only the storm bird; never the witch or a named people.

name: Tokoloshe
looks: A hip-high dwarf-like water spirit that can turn invisible.
behavior: Sent by witch doctors to cause sickness and death; beds are raised on bricks as protection.
license_note: Nguni folk belief.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Still believed by some Zulu and others, and also a satire target. Fine as a small imp; no ethnic dress.

name: Mamlambo
looks: A 20-meter snake with a horse's head, fish tail and short legs, glowing green at night.
behavior: Blamed for deaths in 1997 in the Eastern Cape; rumored to eat faces and brains.
license_note: First dated record is 1997 news: modern origin, folklore age unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. The page calls her a goddess of rivers; living belief with real deaths attached. Listed so the owner sees it.

name: Inkanyamba
looks: A huge dragon-like serpent with a horse head, fins and sometimes wings.
behavior: Said to cause storms, hail and tornadoes when angry.
license_note: Folk belief; age unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. RED: the page calls it a deity and says it must be appeased. Do not use as an enemy.
reads_at_16x20: yes as a storm serpent, but red

name: Mokele-mbembe
looks: A reddish-brown, elephant-sized reptile with a snake-like head, long tail and short legs.
behavior: Lives in riverbank caves, eats plants, and wrecks canoes that come near.
license_note: First recorded 1913 (von Stein); older oral roots unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Cryptid; most experts suggest the rhinoceros as the origin.

name: Kongamato
looks: A winged creature with a 4 to 7 foot wingspan, reddish skin and a toothy beak.
behavior: Haunts rivers and capsizes boats from below.
license_note: First record is Melland, 1923: folklore age unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Cryptid.

name: Kishi
looks: A many-headed man-eater with long tangled hair falling over its faces.
behavior: Destroys a village in the Sudika-mbambi tale; a chief kishi could regrow a cut-off head.
license_note: Chatelain, Folk-tales of Angola, 1894.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Related words mean 'spirit' in several Bantu languages; I could not verify sacred uses, so avoid any mask imagery.

name: Kituta
looks: A river spirit that rules the water and loves great trees and hilltops.
behavior: Common in Mbundu stories; in the passage I read it arises when a character is transformed.
license_note: Werner, 1933; spelling as printed.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. A spirit in living tradition; the dangerous form is unverified, so use only a generic marsh spirit.

name: Kalanoro
looks: A small, hairy, fanged being with backward-facing feet and red-glowing eyes.
behavior: Solitary; some steal, kill or abduct, others serve as healers.
license_note: Folk belief; age unverified.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Said to be linked to ancestors (Vazimba); use only the small forest imp.

name: Aicha Kandicha
looks: A beautiful young woman in white with the legs of a goat or camel.
behavior: Seduces men near water and drives them mad or kills them.
license_note: Oldest cited source is Westermarck, 1926; the link to ancient goddesses is weakly supported.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Hamadsha and Zar societies still hold rites to her; treat as a living spirit. Do not show Moroccan dress.

name: Ghoul
looks: A shapeshifter that lures travelers as a lost relative or old woman, haunting graveyards and deserts.
behavior: Devours travelers and children and eats the dead; in a Lang tale one dines on a fresh corpse.
license_note: Pre-Islamic Arab poetry; Lang preface and the Sidi-Nouman tale.
sensitivity_note: Classed as jinn in Islamic belief; hadith advise the call to prayer for travelers. Use as a desert corpse-eater only.

name: Serpopard
looks: A lioness-bodied creature with a very long serpent neck.
behavior: Shown restrained on Narmer-era palettes, as a symbol of chaos beyond the borders.
license_note: Egyptian and Mesopotamian art, c. 3500 BC onward.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Ancient art motif; no living worship.

name: Ammit
looks: Crocodile head, lion front, hippopotamus back.
behavior: Waits at the scales of judgment to devour impure hearts.
license_note: Ancient Egyptian funerary texts.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Not worshiped as a god, per the page, but part of ancient religion; no Egyptian costume for a faction.

name: Apep
looks: A giant serpent said to be 16 yards long with a flint head.
behavior: Ambushes the sun god's boat each night and uses a magical gaze.
license_note: Ancient Egyptian texts.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. RED: a god of chaos, a deity.

name: Lamashtu
looks: Lion-headed with donkey teeth and bird feet, holding serpents.
behavior: Preys on unborn and newborn babies and mothers; kept off by amulets.
license_note: Cuneiform incantations; Thompson, 1903 (as Labartu).
sensitivity_note: May have been regarded as a goddess in ancient religion, now extinct. Avoid showing harm to infants; use as a marsh hag.

name: Pazuzu
looks: Dog-like muzzle, bulging eyes, gazelle horns, bird talons, wings and scorpion tail.
behavior: Wind demon, evil yet also protective: drove back Lamashtu.
license_note: Evidence from the 8th century BC. A modern film popularized him, but he is ancient.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Ancient religion, now extinct.

name: Humbaba
looks: Mountain-man giant guardian of the cedar forest with seven auras and a terrifying voice.
behavior: Guards the forest until Gilgamesh and Enkidu kill him.
license_note: Old Babylonian Sumerian texts.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Epic figure.
reads_at_16x20: yes: giant with a roaring face

name: Anzu
looks: A huge lion-headed eagle that breathes fire and water.
behavior: Stole the Tablet of Destinies and hid it on a mountain; killed by Ninurta or Marduk.
license_note: Votive relief c. 2550-2500 BC.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Ancient religion, now extinct.

name: Girtablilu
looks: Man's head, torso and arms on a scorpion's body and tail.
behavior: Created by Tiamat in Enuma Elish; guard the gate of Mashu with a deadly glance.
license_note: Ancient art, then Enuma Elish and Gilgamesh.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Ancient religion, now extinct.

name: Mushussu
looks: A scaly dragon with lion forelimbs, eagle hind talons, two horns and a crest.
behavior: A servant beast of Marduk and Nabu.
license_note: Neo-Babylonian art.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. RED: sacred beast of a god (Marduk), though that religion is extinct.

name: Ekimmu
looks: The departed spirit of a dead person who cannot rest.
behavior: Wanders from the underworld seeking food and attaches to those it knew.
license_note: Thompson, 1903.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Ancient religion, now extinct.

name: Alu
looks: A half-man, half-devil hiding in ruins, sometimes without mouth, limbs or ears.
behavior: Slinks through streets and stands over beds to steal sleep.
license_note: Thompson, 1903.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Ancient religion, now extinct.

name: Div
looks: Gigantic horned beings with boar-like tusks; the White Div is as huge as a mountain.
behavior: Crave human flesh, use sorcery and serve Ahriman; foes of Rostam.
license_note: Avesta daeva and Shahnameh.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Daeva belong to Zoroastrian tradition, which is still practiced; keep it a monster, not a religious depiction.

name: Zahhak
looks: A tyrant with two black snakes growing from his shoulders.
behavior: The snakes must be fed human brains; Fereydun chains him under Mount Damavand.
license_note: Avesta and Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Avestan demon in Zoroastrian text; fine as a monster.

name: Simurgh
looks: A huge bird with a peacock body, dog's head and lion's claws.
behavior: Benevolent mediator; hostile only to snakes.
license_note: Avesta and Shahnameh.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Benevolent in its tradition; no real dangerous form, so it fails rule 3. Not an enemy; maybe a rare ally.

name: Manticore
looks: Human face, lion body, scorpion tail, three rows of teeth.
behavior: Eats victims whole, leaving no bones.
license_note: Ctesias, 5th century BC, via later Greek writers.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Widely used in fiction. Whether the D&D SRD lists it was not checked (unverified); the folklore license is green regardless.
reads_at_16x20: yes: lion with a stinging tail

name: Karkadann
looks: A buffalo-sized beast with a single nose horn, based on the rhinoceros.
behavior: Fierce toward other animals, even elephants.
license_note: Al-Biruni (973-1048).
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Not sacred.

name: Roc
looks: A bird large enough to seize elephants.
behavior: Drops elephants from a height; its egg appears in the Aladdin tale.
license_note: Arabian Nights, Marco Polo (1298).
sensitivity_note: Folk and literary; widely used in fiction. Lang's text shows the egg only.

name: Ifrit
looks: A powerful jinn of smoke and fire.
behavior: Vengeful and proud; can offer help or harm.
license_note: Quran (an-Naml) and hadith.
sensitivity_note: Jinn are part of Islamic belief. Use as a generic fire monster, never with Muslim imagery.

name: Nasnas
looks: A half-human with half a head, one arm and one leg.
behavior: Hops quickly through the desert.
license_note: Lane described it; some Shia texts use it to disparage opponents.
sensitivity_note: Unverified, one source. Occasionally used to disparage a religious group, so avoid sectarian dress.
